newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yield at Wed Russia T-bill sale seen near market.
newsitem.headline: Yield at Wed Russia T-bill sale seen near market.

text.p: Short-term Russian government securities to be auctioned on Wednesday will likely be sold at prices slightly above market levels, given increased appetite for the bills, traders said on Tuesday.
They said the Finance Ministry, which needs to raise a huge 10 trillion roubles to pay bills maturing on Wednesday, would benefit from a falling yield trend which the market expects to continue.
ON WEDNESDAY
The Finance Ministry sells:
*9.00 trln rbls 105-day T-bill (series 21074)
*5.50 trln rbls 364-day T-bill (series 21075)
The Finance Ministry pays/repays:
*10.47 trln rbls 154-day T-bill (series 22066)
*284.62 bln rbls in interest on OFZ (series 24007)
ON TUESDAY
*Average yield fell to 19.87 pct from 20.15 pct
*Turnover rose to 5.34 bln rbls from 3.58 bln rbls
*The Central Bank sold 195.3 bln rbls in T-bills, OFZ and VSM bonds

Dealers forecast the average yield on series 21074 bill, maturing on September 24, 1997, to be in the 15.85-19.26 percent range. Series 22060 bills, maturing on September 17, 1997, the closest maturity date to the new issue, closed on Tuesday at 95.80 to yield 16.16 percent.

Dealers forecast the average yield on series 21075 bill, maturing on June 10, 1998, to be in the 20.49-21.03 percent range. The series 23007 bills, maturing on May 20, 1998, closed on Tuesday at 83.58 percent to yield 20.85 percent.
On Wednesday the Finance Ministry will first auction nine trillion roubles of 105-day paper, against the 10 trillion it must repay.
One dealer said that foreigners who prefer longer paper and are likely to keep prices in the second auction of 364-day paper low would not compete for the short-term paper.
"The Finance Ministry hopes to get most funds for repayment from the first auction, and as non-residents are usually indifferent to it, Russian banks can be aggressive," the dealer said.
But the trader said the lack of foreign demand appeared to be outweighed by a general interest in government paper.
"At today's trading no one sold. No one expected to buy at better prices tomorrow and that's why the demand for the short paper may also be high."
--Anna Smirnova, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
